cards.explanation: The answer is the fortress of Ecbatana. The search starts in the archives in Babylon, but the scroll is found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media (Ezra 6:2). The search started in one city and the scroll turned up in another. That memo is the one that mentions Cyrus's decree.

The answer is sacrifices. The memo says, "Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices…" (Ezra 6:3). This house is built for worship, not just to look pretty on a hill. Cyrus put it in writing, and now it's in the memo, friends.

The answer is False. The memo says, "The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury." (Ezra 6:4). The Jews don't pay the building costs themselves. Think of a contractor who hands you the plans and then says the invoice goes to somebody else.

The answer is the gold and silver articles. The memo says the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple, must be returned to the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:5). They are to be deposited in the house of God. That's the order, and it names exactly what Nebuchadnezzar carried to Babylon.

The answer is "Stay away from that place." Darius opens with, "You must stay away from that place!" (Ezra 6:6). No small talk and no warm-up, friends. Tattenai asked questions, and the king answers with a firm hands-off.

The answer is hindered. The cost is paid in full from the royal treasury "…so that the work will not be hindered." (Ezra 6:8). The money comes out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates. The aim of the decree is plain, bakers: keep the work moving.

The answer is priests. The supplies are given daily, "…as requested by the priests in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 6:9). The priests ask, and the supplies come, daily and without fail. That's one steady delivery, friends.

The answer is True. Darius says the sacrifices let them offer a sweet aroma to the God of heaven "…and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons." (Ezra 6:10). It's right there in the decree. He covers the supplies and asks for prayer too.

The answer is that it becomes a pile of rubble. Darius says, "…his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense." (Ezra 6:11). It's a serious warning, and that's one heavy part of this passage, friends. Darius wants no one touching that decree.

The answer is to destroy this house of God. Darius says, "May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 6:12). Both altering the decree and destroying the house are covered. He's guarding that house on every side, bakers.

The answer is True. The text says Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai and their associates "…diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed." (Ezra 6:13). No dragging their feet and no grumbling in the record, friends. They did exactly what the king said.

The answer is Haggai and Zechariah. The elders built and prospered "…through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo." (Ezra 6:14). Two prophets, one building. They had backup from the Lord's own messengers, bakers.

The answer is God. They finished "…according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia." (Ezra 6:14). God's command comes first in the list, friends. The kings' decrees come after it.

The answer is the sixth year of King Darius. The temple was completed on the third day of Adar "…in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius." (Ezra 6:15). The work is done, bakers, with every stone and timber in place. That's a finished house.

The answer is one for each tribe of Israel. The sin offering was "…twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel." (Ezra 6:17). It was a sin offering for all Israel. Every tribe is counted, friends.

The answer is False. They appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups "…according to what is written in the Book of Moses." (Ezra 6:18). Darius's decree covered money and supplies (Ezra 6:8-9). The assignments came from the Book of Moses, not from the king.

The answer is that they purified themselves. "All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean." (Ezra 6:20). Purified is the word the text uses for them, friends. The same verse goes on to say the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb.

The answer is the Levites. "…the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves." (Ezra 6:20). They took care of it for the exiles, the priests and themselves. The Levites are the ones the text names for the job, bakers. That's a big job on a big day.

The answer is False. The Israelites who returned from exile ate it "…together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel." (Ezra 6:21). Those who sought the LORD joined them. It's a bigger table than the statement said, friends.

The answer is that the LORD made them joyful. They kept the feast with joy "…because the LORD had made them joyful…" (Ezra 6:22). The joy came from the LORD Himself, friends. It's the kind of joy you can't bake yourself, and I've tried.
